title: The Lie Most Leaders Believe That Could Cost Them Their Job
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Dempsey challenges the comforting claim that human judgment and soft skills will protect leaders from AI replacement. He uses an expected-value argument, showing that an AI system can be far less accurate than a person and still be economically preferable if each decision costs a fraction as much. He supports this with a list of human error statistics, including a claimed 4 trillion dollars in annual US losses from human mistakes. His leadership prescription is to think like the systems that may replace you: make many small bets, watch for tiny signals, add AI to micro-tasks, build learning loops and prize speed of adaptation over prediction. The framing is deliberately provocative and the numbers are rhetorical illustrations, but the practical advice is a coherent approach to leading change with AI rather than being led by it.
points: The comfort that human judgment is the differentiator is challenged by the poor track record of human decision-making.
An expected-value comparison shows AI can be much less accurate than a human and still be worth using because decisions are so much cheaper.
Large organisations will apply this arithmetic to cut roles, while a smaller leader can apply the same thinking to get better outcomes and momentum.
The five moves, small bets, tiny signals, micro-integrations, learning loops and speed of adaptation, give leaders a concrete way to start.
The stated goal is for leaders to design AI-human collaboration systems themselves rather than have them imposed.
quotes: The recurrent theme about why AI can't possibly replace humans is because it lacks judgement. In this line of thinking, human judgement is superior to machine judgement. But is this true?
Because an AI system can be a significantly worse decision-maker than a human and still be worth using.
Here's the crucial insight: While big organizations use this math to cut workforces, yours probably doesn't.
Here's the punch line: You need to learn to think, act, and lead like the systems that are being created to replace you.
Start with 10-minute tasks, not 10-hour projects. You're learning to work the way AI-human collaboration systems actually function.
The leaders who win aren't the ones who guess right about where AI is going. They're the ones who adapt fastest when AI capabilities change.

This changes how you think about every decision you make as a leader. Which meetings actually need your judgment versus which could be handled by AI analysis? Which strategic planning processes are worth your time versus which are just expensive theater?
